runs.text: os meninos fazem correr, tirando lhe às

lines.note: This continues f166's straw ring: children make it roll and shoot at it. The moving target explains the otherwise ambiguous object name `Fama`.
`Famauo iru` means shooting at the ring. Portuguese repeats the children's action; `me-` continues as `meninos` below.

runs.text: ninos a este circulo de palha com frechas.

lines.note: The target is explicitly the straw ring, and the projectiles are arrows. This rules out interpreting the preceding play as a ball game.

runs.text: Arco com que tirão a eſte

lines.note: `Famayumi` is the bow used for shooting at that ring. The compound's second part is 弓, not a separate verb.
`circulo` closes the bow definition by referring back to the ring. It is a physical continuation, not new vocabulary.
`Famabata` and `Miguiua` identify the shore's edge. The mechanical reading ミギワ reflects the printed spelling rather than requiring modern みぎわ notation in Level 1.
`Famabe` has the same meaning as the immediately preceding shore-edge entry. `Idem` does not refer back to the children's target.

runs.text: Terra que eſta aolongo do mar

lines.note: `Famabiſaxi` is coastal land with a particular eroded formation. The following line explains what the waves have done to it.
Waves have worn and hollowed out the land. This physical description is more specific than simply a beach or coastline.
`Famabô` denotes a small tree or large herb growing at the beach. The botanical identification needs the following medicinal and regional information.

runs.text: grande da praya que he boa pera lauatorio dos

lines.note: The plant is useful for washing the feet. This is the dictionary's reported use, not a modern recommendation or proof of species identity.
The Indian name `Nigunde` is supplied as a comparison. It is not Japanese, and an exact modern botanical identification needs an external source.
`Famabutçu` is a plant with a regional alternative name. `cami` refers to the upper-region usage, not a deity in this phrase.
The alternative is `Cauara yomogui`, 河原蓬. This identifies the lexical relationship without changing the regional headword's spelling.
`Famachi` is a sea fish, compatible with はまち. The brief gloss alone does not establish a precise modern size or age category.
`Famachidori` is a shore bird, rendered by Portuguese `Maſſarico`. Treat that as the compiler's bird comparison, not a modern taxonomic equivalence.
The bird frequents beaches. This completes the habitat description and supports the 浜 compound.
`Famaguiua` means the edge of the beach. `gui` is hard ギ here, contrasting with bare `gi` in the historical ヂ series.
`Famaguri` is ハマグリ; Portuguese `Ameijoas` gives clams. The bilingual match is straightforward but does not settle every zoological distinction.
`Famanadexico` names a plant. The gloss only says “an herb,” so the compound 浜撫子 is a reading aid, not a confirmed species identification.
`Famari` describes sinking or becoming deeply lodged. The Portuguese examples below distinguish this from the modern abstract sense alone.

runs.text: muito como na lama, caua, poço &c. ¶

lines.note: Mud, a pit, and a well are places one may become embedded. `Do-` begins the Japanese mud example.
`Do- / toni famaru` means becoming stuck in mud. `Ali-` begins an editorial marker for the following metaphorical extension.
`Xeqenno cotoni famaru` is becoming absorbed in worldly affairs. `permet.` marks metaphorical use, not a Japanese word.

runs.text: Eſtar muito metido nas couſas do mundo.

lines.note: The Portuguese says being deeply involved in worldly things. This confirms the figurative, rather than muddy or physical, reading of the example.
`Acuni famaru` means being immersed in evil. The Portuguese uses the moral category of sins in the continuation.
`metido nos peccados` completes involvement in sins. This is the moral extension of becoming trapped or embedded.

runs.text: Hũa erua dagoa doce como ca-

lines.note: `Famauogui` denotes a freshwater plant resembling reeds. The spelling gives ハマヲギ, but the short gloss does not resolve an exact species.
`ca- / niços` completes “reeds.” The line is the end of the plant comparison, not another entry.

runs.text: Dar de comer a bois, & beſ-

lines.note: `Famaxe` means feeding cattle or other beasts. The causative relationship to animal eating is clearer when read with the example below.
`Vmani cutçuuauo famaſuru` literally puts the bit into the horse's mouth. This extends the feeding/holding-in-the-mouth sense rather than describing actual food.
Portuguese explains putting the bridle on the horse. It confirms the tack-related interpretation of `cutçuuauo` above.
`Famayumi` is a small bow used by children. It repeats as a headword the compound illustrated near the top of this page.
The cross-reference `Fama` points to the ring-target game. It should not be interpreted as the beach homograph.
`Fame` is the transitive counterpart of fitting or sinking something in. The gloss begins with putting or embedding an object.
Mud, a pit, and a well repeat the physical settings of `Famari`. `Item` introduces a constructional use with another verb.

runs.text: outro verbo, encaxar algum pao em outro. Vt,

lines.note: The compound describes fitting one piece of wood into another. Portuguese explicitly signals that another verb participates.
`Yerifamuru` and `qirifamuru` are fitting-related compounds; their exact first elements deserve lexical caution. `Yauo` starts an arrow example continued below.
`Yauo famuru` is setting an arrow on the bow. The Portuguese identifies the object and action without requiring an eating interpretation of `famu`.
`Famecuſa` means fill or rubble. The compiler explicitly says another form is the proper word, supplied on the next line.
`Vmecuſa` ウメクサ is that preferred form. The dictionary's correction remains a cross-reference, not permission to erase `Famecuſa`.
`Yabure foroburu` explains 破滅, destruction. The headword's final `-t` represents a historical checked ending, not a lost following vowel to restore.

runs.text: Comer de animaes como de bois, ou ca-

lines.note: This nominal `Fami` is animal eating. Cattle are one example, and the list continues below.
Horses and birds complete the animal list. The line belongs to the feeding sense, not the following bit-in-the-mouth noun.
`Cutçuuano cucumi` identifies the mouth-held part of a bit. `Fami` here names tack rather than the act of eating.

runs.text: ou ferro que entra na boca do cauallo.

lines.note: The iron enters the horse's mouth. This completes the anatomical location of the bit component.
The verbal `Fami, u, ǒda` describes animals eating. Read the Portuguese animals as the eaters in context, confirmed by the bird example across the column break.
`Toriga yeuo famu` is “the birds eat food.” The subject marker `ga` removes the ambiguity that Portuguese infinitival wording might create.
`Os paſſa- / ros comem` completes “the birds eat.” It confirms that birds are the agents, not the food.
`Famicayeri` describes wild boars returning to feed. The reason for the return is specified in the next lines.

runs.text: monteſes a buſcar o paſto que lhes tinhão posto

lines.note: They seek food that has been put out for them. The final phrase identifies that food as bait.
`negaça` marks the lure or bait. This makes the example a hunting context rather than ordinary husbandry.

runs.text: Comida de beſtas, ou de paſſaros.

lines.note: `Famimono` is food for beasts or birds. The noun is built around animal feeding, consistent with the preceding family.
`Famo` is a fish name, compatible with ハモ. No further species details are printed in this very short definition.

runs.text: O que vai mariſcar à praya.

lines.note: `Famǒdo` names someone gathering shellfish on the shore. The shore-worker interpretation depends on the full gloss, not the long-vowel hint alone.

runs.text: Item, O que trabalha nas marinhas.

lines.note: The term also applies to a worker in saltworks (`marinhas`). This broadens the occupation beyond shellfish gathering.

runs.text: Famuqi, u, uita. i, Mucai, cǒ.

lines.note: `Famuqi` is glossed by facing or confronting. The printed `Mucai, cǒ` has an unusual abbreviated paradigm; do not mechanically normalize it from modern morphology.
The encounter is in war. This supplies the adversarial context for the preceding facing verb.
`Famure` describes birds beating or striking. The next line identifies wings and water as the relevant objects.

runs.text: darem com as aſas na agoa.

lines.note: Birds strike the water with their wings. This is a wing-beating action, not an unspecified fight among birds.
`Famuxa` is an ordinary soldier, compatible with 葉武者. The definition concerns rank rather than an individual warrior's name.
`Fan` is 飯, cooked rice. `Iy` is the accompanying Japanese gloss for rice, not Portuguese or an inflection of `Fan`.

runs.text: Nones, contrario de Chô, que he pa-

lines.note: This `Fan` is the odd-number category opposed to `Chô`, even. It differs from the rice homograph immediately above.

runs.text: res. ¶ Item, A metade, mas não ſe vſa ſe-

lines.note: The line completes “even numbers,” then introduces the half sense. The compiler qualifies how that latter meaning is used.

runs.text: não com algũa compoſição, ou de pois de outra

lines.note: “Half” occurs in compounds or after another word. This is a grammatical usage restriction, not a ban on the preceding odd-number sense.
`Fanbun` is 半分, “a half,” illustrating the compound use. The Portuguese equivalent is direct.
`Fitotçu fan` means one and a half. It illustrates `fan` following a quantity rather than forming a single lexical headword.
This `Fan` is a signature or mark on a letter. `Fanuo ſu-` begins the act of placing that mark.
`ſu- / yuru` completes the placing verb. Portuguese equates it with signing one's name or putting one's mark.
This `Fan` is a printing block or impression. The following Japanese expressions concern producing or printing it, not signing a letter.
Join `fi- / raqu` and `ſuritçuqu- / ru` across the boundaries. The listed verbs concern opening/issuing, carving, raising, and printing in the block-printing context.
`ru` completes the final Japanese verb, followed by “print.” It is a continuation of the list, not a separate verb entry.
`Fana` is 鼻 here. `Fanauo camu` means blowing the nose; its Portuguese translation is divided across the next line.
`A- / ſoarſe` finishes blowing the nose. `Fanauo ſuſuru` then means sniffing mucus inward, a contrasting action.
The mucus belongs to the nose. `Fanauo fiqu` begins a sneezing example, whose gloss continues below.
`Eſpir- / rar` completes sneezing. `Fanauo xicamuru` is wrinkling the nose, not the preceding action repeated.
`Fanauo tacǒ ſuru` literally raises the nose and figuratively means becoming proud. The adverbial form belongs to 高く, not a separate noun.
The pride gloss ends here. `Fanauo tçugu` is then explained as falling out of a lord's favor; do not force the idiom into its literal nasal meaning.
The lord's displeasure completes that idiom. `Fanaga taru` begins the next example, a running nose.

runs.text: rer o ranho dos narizes: mas fana perſi não ſe

lines.note: The Portuguese explicitly warns that `fana` by itself does not mean mucus, despite the running-nose phrase. This lexical caveat should survive the commentary.
The warning concludes, followed by `Fanauo ſoroyuru`. Literally aligning noses is explained as horses standing together.
Many horses together finish that image. `Fanaqire-` begins a separate figurative expression continued below.

runs.text: Vaca forra. i, Peſſoa que anda liure,

lines.note: The questionable `vji` remains as printed; expected 牛 would suggest `vxi`. The Portuguese explains a free cow, then a free-ranging person; `Peſſoa...` is Portuguese and is rendered italic accordingly.

runs.text: & à vontade como vaca q̃ ſe lhe cortou a põ-

lines.note: The person goes freely like a cow whose tethering part has been cut. This explains the metaphor rather than asserting a modern proverb identification.

runs.text: ta do beiço por onde eſtaua amarrada.

lines.note: The cut is at the lip where the animal was tied. That physical detail connects freedom to the nose-cut expression above.
Now `Fana` means 花, a flower or rose. `Fanaga chiru` is flowers falling or scattering, distinct from the preceding nose vocabulary.
The flowers fall or scatter. `Fa-` starts the transitive counterpart on the following line.
`Fanauo chiraſu` is scattering flowers. `Item` introduces a figurative action whose scope must be read below.
The figurative sense includes fighting valiantly and gallantly. It is not simply a literal flower-scattering ceremony.
Another skillful or well-executed action can also be meant. `Fa-` then begins the next flower-arranging example.
`Fanauo tatçuru` means setting up a bouquet. The vessel holding it is named in the following line.

runs.text: hum vaſo, a que chamão Quaſin. ¶

lines.note: The vessel is called `Quaſin`, a Japanese term within Portuguese prose. This concludes the arrangement example and starts the next one.
`Fanauo voru` is picking flowers with the stalk. The final `Fa-` belongs to the subsequent intransitive example.
`Fanaga xibomu` is a flower withering or shriveling. Portuguese `Engelharſe` supports the loss-of-freshness sense, not another picking action.
